headline.main: Exploiting the Arctic?: "What Trump Wants to Do with Greenland Is a Mystery to Me"
headline.social: Exploiting the Arctic?: "What Trump Wants to Do with Greenland Is a Mystery to Me"

intro: U.S. President Donald Trump has cast a covetous gaze at Greenland. But why? In an interview, Greenland expert Paul Bierman explains why the exploitation of natural resources on the island is difficult, expensive and has generally not been profitable.
text:
DER SPIEGEL: Professor Bierman, U.S. President Donald Trump has been talking about Greenland for years. Apparently, he now wants to incorporate it into the U.S. "one way or another," as he recently said in his speech to Congress. Why does Trump want Greenland so badly?
Paul Bierman: I don't know. What President Trump wants to do with Greenland is a mystery to me.
DER SPIEGEL: Perhaps he is interested in exploiting the island’s natural resources?
Bierman: I don't know whether Trump has thought this idea through. Greenland has fascinated people for many centuries. It is a mystical place. And the mineral and raw material deposits under and next to Greenland’s ice have become part of this myth. For decades there has been a lot of talk about extracting Greenland's raw materials. But they are often fantasies. Most of these ideas are never realized and nothing much happens in the end.
DER SPIEGEL: How many mines are in operation there?
Bierman: There are currently two active mines in Greenland. Several others have been closed, and a number of other projects have never come to fruition. Often, this has not been because companies were prohibited from opening mines. Rather, they have had countless opportunities to exploit Greenland's natural resources, but have generally decided against doing so after realizing it wouldn’t be worth the investment.
DER SPIEGEL: Why not?
Bierman: Contrary to what people say, Greenland is not unique in terms of mineral resources. The geology is similar to that found in Arctic Canada and other parts of North America. You can find a lot of minerals in Greenland, but few deposits are exceptional. And if there is something special, it is rarely present in both high concentrations and in a place that’s accessible.
DER SPIEGEL: In other words, for every ton of raw material extracted, a lot of other material has to be removed? And the effort does not justify the return?
Bierman: Exactly right. It is extremely expensive, complex and time-consuming to extract, transport and process raw materials in Greenland. The conditions are extreme. First, workers have to work for months in the winter without daylight, in arctic weather with temperatures of 40 degrees below zero along with snowstorms and frozen ground. Secondly, the deposits are often hundreds of kilometers away from settlements and transportation hubs. Before extracting raw materials on the island, you must first build extensive infrastructure and both supply and logistics chains. In large parts of Greenland, there are no overland roads, no large ports, and when there is thick fog for days, not even a helicopter can land. Lastly, you need a large number of highly specialized workers ...
DER SPIEGEL: ... and Greenland has fewer than 60,000 inhabitants ...
Bierman: ... meaning workers with specialized skills are rare in the country. That means companies have to bring in specialists from Europe, the U.S. or Asia at great cost to train a local work force. On top of that, climate change will make mining even more difficult.
DER SPIEGEL: Why is that? It is widely assumed that the melting ice will make it easier to access the raw materials.
Bierman: If you build on the permafrost, which is ubiquitous in Greenland – whether it’s buildings, roads or rails – you will have a problem as soon as it thaws. The ground will literally melt away beneath your feet.
DER SPIEGEL: The Thule Air Base, belonging to the U.S., has been suffering from this problem for decades. Buildings sink and tilt and cracks have developed in the runway.
Bierman: In addition, the thawing of the ground or the retreat of glaciers can lead to massive rockfalls or worse, such as in September 2023, when a side of a mountain in Dickson Fjord in northwest Greenland collapsed and triggered a tsunami about 200 meters high, which then sloshed back and forth in the fjord for days. Fortunately, the area is remote and was deserted at the time. But near an oil platform, a mine or a workers' settlement, such a monster wave could lead to a catastrophe. And finally, climate change can make Greenland's ports unusable.
DER SPIEGEL: How so?
Bierman: As the Greenland ice sheet melts, the weight pressing down the land mass beneath and next to the ice decreases. As a result, the land gradually rises, as do the port areas.
DER SPIEGEL: At the same time, sea levels are rising around the world as a result of Greenland ice sheet melting.
Bierman: It is estimated that the coast of Greenland could rise by 1.80 meters per century – four times as fast as the current rate of sea level rise.
DER SPIEGEL: Trump is clearly targeting minerals containing rare earth elements, which have also been a focus of his demands from Ukraine. Why are rare earth elements so important to him?
Bierman: I don't understand what Trump, of all people, wants to do with rare earth elements. One major use of them, for example, is in the construction of electric cars and wind turbines. But Trump clearly has no interest in wind farms and electric cars.
DER SPIEGEL: Would it be easier to extract these raw materials in Ukraine?
Bierman: In Ukraine, too, many rare earth deposits are undeveloped and still years away from extraction. But it would be much easier there than in the frigid and remote Arctic. There is infrastructure in Ukraine: interurban roads, nationwide energy networks, established industrial structures, experienced workers. Greenland has none of that.
DER SPIEGEL: But there is a rare earth mining project in Greenland that has been in the planning stages for years ...
Bierman: ... and which has not yet started. There’s no question: There are significant deposits of rare earth elements in Greenland. These are often found in rocks called pegmatites, veins composed of various rare minerals. These pegmatites, though, have one major disadvantage: They often contain radioactive elements, particularly uranium. And Greenland's government has banned the mining of uranium.
DER SPIEGEL: Could the oil and natural gas deposits off the coast of Greenland be of interest to Trump?
Bierman: There are studies that suggest that there is some potential for oil and gas. But here too, the extraction costs would probably be exceptionally high. In addition, the risk of collisions with icebergs is increasing with climate change as the ice sheet shrinks. Don't forget: The Titanic was also hit by an iceberg from Greenland. And above all, the Greenlanders have forbidden drilling off their coast.
DER SPIEGEL: The U.S. had military bases in Greenland during the Cold War because of its proximity to the Soviet Union. Do you think the island’s strategic location explains Trump’s interest in Greenland?
Bierman: I don't think so. The U.S. once had almost a dozen military bases in Greenland, all of them, with the exception of the one in Thule, have been abandoned. A few hundred people are still stationed there, perhaps 150 of them are military personnel. If the place is deemed to be of strategic importance, the military presence could once again be increased. But I have the impression that Trump is primarily interested in flexing his muscles. He doesn't recognize the true and immense value that Greenland has for humanity.
DER SPIEGEL: Which is?
Bierman: Greenland's greatest value is as an ice reservoir: a frozen carapace that is sometimes more than 3,000 meters thick. If that ice melts, global sea levels will rise by another seven meters. Coastal cities around the world – Miami, Shanghai, Hamburg – would flood. Tens of millions, perhaps hundreds of millions of people will be displaced, at a cost of thousands of billions of dollars. We should be protecting Greenland and its ice, not exploiting it.
